extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers in media studies, journalists and communications professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Define and analyze 'media events' and 'pseudo-events' — their characteristics, types, historical examples, authenticity issues, and how they function in contemporary (including social) media. Useful for media studies summaries, coursework, or introductory reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic definition of media event / pseudo-event
rubrics_metrics.description: A media event, also known as a pseudo-event, is an event, activity, or experience conducted for the purpose of creating media publicity; it may also be any event that is covered in the mass media or was hosted largely with the media in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the working definitional criterion: purpose (create publicity) and/or being hosted with media in mind. Examples include events deliberately organized to attract coverage rather than arising spontaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katz & Dayan defining characteristics (ceremonial 'media events')
rubrics_metrics.description: Media events (as theorized by Katz and Dayan) are ceremonial events with narrative progression that are live broadcast and gather a large segment of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key characteristics to check for: immediacy (broadcast live), organized by a non-media entity, containing ceremonial and dramatic value, preplanning, and focusing on a personality (single person or group). Classic examples: royal weddings, funerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media event immediacy and liveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A defining characteristic is that it is immediate (i.e., it is broadcast live).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the event is intended to be consumed live or in real time; live broadcast/liveness increases the event's media-event qualities and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization by non-media entity
rubrics_metrics.description: Media events are often organized by a non-media entity rather than by media producers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the origin: whether an organization, institution, politician, or other non-media actor staged the event with media coverage in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial/dramatic value and narrative progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Media events have ceremonial and dramatic value and a narrative progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the event is staged to produce a clear narrative arc, drama, or ceremonial spectacle that media can package and replay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Media events often focus on a personality, whether a single person or a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the event's framing centers on an individual or group persona (e.g., political leader, celebrity) as the story's anchor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boorstin's pseudo-event characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A pseudo-event (Boorstin) is planned, planted, or incited; characteristics include being dramatic, repeatable, costly, intellectually planned, and social; it causes other pseudo-events, and one must know about it to be considered 'informed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Boorstin's checklist to judge pseudo-event-ness: Is the event manufactured for publicity? Is it staged/repeatable and costly? Does it generate further manufactured events or status through shared knowledge?

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as a substitute for advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of paying for advertising time, a media or pseudo-event seeks to use public relations to gain media and public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the tactic: whether actors rely on PR strategies (staging events, leaks, photo-ops) to obtain earned media rather than paid promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: News conference as a media-event type
rubrics_metrics.description: News conferences are often held when an organization wants members of the press to get an announcement simultaneously; in-person events may include interviews, questioning, and show-and-tell, but often provide little information or don't reach a clear consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a news conference as a media event, note simultaneous press access, potential lack of substantive information, interactive Q&A, and expectations around certain institutions (e.g., sports leagues). Example: NFL-required postgame press availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political conventions and planned political presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Political conventions, planned presentations or speeches about company earnings or political issues are a form of media event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for orchestrated political staging intended to generate news coverage and manage political narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity events as orchestrated narrative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Award ceremonies, red carpet events and celebrity photo opportunities are media events where the event is orchestrated to introduce a chosen narrative into the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether celebrity events are designed primarily to construct or reinforce a public narrative or image rather than inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leak-staged 'sex tapes' as pseudo-events
rubrics_metrics.description: When created with the intention of being 'leaked,' sex tapes are a form of pseudo-event because their purpose is to generate media attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider intentional leaking as a deliberate publicity tactic; examine production and dissemination intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protests and charity events staged for media attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Protests and charity events may be planned almost exclusively for the purpose of getting media attention for an issue or cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize activist or charity events for instrumental staging aimed at visibility rather than spontaneous grassroots action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity concerns / PR-driven stylistic content
rubrics_metrics.description: These events are used by public relations professionals to satisfy journalists’ interests and needs so they can create a great story; this technique has been criticized for not producing authentic material, which is seen as stylistic instead of substantial informational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ethical and epistemic implications: does the event prioritize image/story over substantive information? Does it risk undermining trust in media coverage?

rubrics_metrics.name: Tourism pseudo-events and hyperreality
rubrics_metrics.description: Tourism is subject to pseudo-events that are often staged attractions or activities presented as 'authentic' but are hyperreal symbols rather than true reflections of local life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing tourism experiences, identify staged performances, actors/characters, and commodified symbols that create an illusion of authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrities as 'human pseudo-events' (manufactured image)
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrities have an image that represents an ideal life and elite status separate from everyday life; they can create pseudo-events (autograph signings, appearances, charity projects) that function as manufactured publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate celebrity actions as performative events designed to sustain or craft public persona and media narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-scientific internet polls as pseudo-events
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-scientific internet polls are self-selected, used to invite mass participation, drive traffic, and can be mistaken for legitimate scientific polls, improving the image being reported rather than providing substantive news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such polls skeptically: check sampling method, potential for manipulation or agenda-setting, and whether they serve to generate engagement rather than reliable information.

rubrics_metrics.name: War coverage and the simulacra critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Televised or heavily mediated war coverage (e.g., the Gulf War) can be argued to have become media events to the point of simulation, raising debates about whether such coverage reflects reality or constructs a media reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to interrogate whether coverage is a mediated spectacle that may distort substantive realities; consider claims from postmodern critiques (Baudrillard) about simulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological and historical conditions enabling media events
rubrics_metrics.description: Media events became practical with communications technologies (telegraph, daily newspapers) and later the internet, which enabled same-day news cycles, live publishing, real-time social media coverage and immediate analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the infrastructural enabling factors (media technology, distribution channels) that make an event function as a media event in its historical moment.
